book_title:
Salomon's Canticle of Canticles
which in Hebrew is called Sir Hasirim. שיר השירים

intros.title: THE ARGUMENT OF THE CANTICLE OF CANTICLES.
intros.text:
SALOMON, called also Ecclesiastes, and Idida, according to these three names (as S. Jerome [1] noteth) writ three books of three particular arguments, directed to three degrees of people, [2] with three distinct titles, all tending to one end, the true service of God, which bringeth to eternal felicity. In the first he teacheth the principles of good life, to fly from vices, and follow virtues:
belonging to such as begin to observe God's law, wherein true wisdom consisteth: and this book is called the Proverbs, or Parables, that is to say, Pithy, brief, sententious precepts, of Salomon, which signifieth Pacificus, Peaceable, or Pacifier: the son of David, King of Israel. In the second he [3] exhorteth to contemn this world, shewing that true felicity consisteth not in any worldly or temporal things, but in the eternal fruition of God, which is obtained by keeping his commandments. And this book he entitleth: The words of Ecclesiastes, which is Concionator, Preacher, Son of David, King of Jerusalem, because he there exhorteth such as have made some [4] progress in virtues, called Proficients, signified by the inhabitants of the Metropolitan city Jerusalem; whereas in the former he styled himself King of Israel, proposing precepts meet for all the twelve tribes, and all vulgar men desirous and beginning to serve God: In both books, for more authority sake, making mention of his godly renowned father the Royal Prophet David, with his own title also of King. But in this third book he only expresseth his proper name Salomon, whom God singularly loved, whereof he was called Idida. Because this alone, without mention of [5] father or King, was most convenient for the Perfect, who not as servants, or young scholars are moved by fear of authority, but as children are sweetly drawn by love. And this he writ in verse, entitling it not simply a Canticle, but The Canticle of Canticles, as preeminent above other [6] Canticles: The bridal song for the Marriage, to be solemnized between God himself and his glorious spouse. For though all holy Scriptures are the spiritual bread, and food of the faithful, yet all [7] are not meat for all, at all seasons. Some parts are not for sinners, nor for beginners, nor for such as are yet in the way towards perfection, but only for the perfect. According to the Apostle's doctrine: Milk is for children, that are yet unskillful of the word of justice. But strong meat is for the perfect, [8] them that by custom, have their senses exercised to the discerning of good and evil. With what moderation therefore and humility, this Canticle of God's perfect spouse may be read, the discreet will consider, and not presume above their reach, but be wise with sobriety. For here be very high and hidden Mysteries, as Origen teacheth in his learned Commentaries (which Saint Jerome translated into Latin and singularly commendeth) and so much harder to be rightly understood, for that the fervent spiritual love, of the inward man, reformed in soul, and perfected in spirit, is here uttered in the same usual words and terms, wherewith natural, worldly, yea and carnal love of the outward man, old Adam, corrupted by sin, is commonly expressed: and are so much more dangerous to be mistaken, as we are more addicted to proper will, & private judgement, or subject to carnal, or passionate motions. Wherefore it seemeth most meet to keep the same order in [9] reading these three books, which the author wise Salomon observed in writing them. And which Philosophers also follow in their form of discipline. For they first learn and teach Moral Philosophy, then Natural & lastly Metaphysics, which is their Divinity. As Salomon had given them example: first teaching precepts of good life and manners, in his Proverbs: after, discoursing of natural things in Ecclesiastes, deduced thence a conclusion, which profane Philosophers well understood not, to contemn this world: and finally cometh to high mystical Divinity, in this supereminent Canticle: written in another style, in verse, and in form of a sacred Dialogue between Christ and his spouse, or as Origen calleth it, in form of an Interlude, in respect of [10] [11] diverse speakers & actors, & of diverse persons, to whom the speeches are directed, and of whom they are uttered. For by the Spouse or Bridegroom, is not only understood Christ as Man, but [12] also as God, and the whole Blessed Trinity; to whom many prayers, praises and thanks are offered up; and by whom many benefits are given, praises returned, & promises made to his spouse. Likewise by the Spouse or Bride the ancient fathers understand three sorts of spouses: all [13] espoused to Christ, and to God, to wit, his General Spouse, the whole Church of the old and [14] new Testaments: of all that are, and shall be perfect, making one mystical body, free from sin, without spot or wrinkle, sanctified in Christ. Also his special spouse, which is every [15] [16] particular holy soul. And his singular spouse, his most blessed & most immaculate Virgin [17] Mother. This being the general sum of this excellent Canticle, remitting the reader, for explication thereof to the learned devout Commenters, both of ancient and late writers, we shall also [18] endeavour to gather the same contents more particularly, not before the chapters, because we cannot there so conveniently distinguish the same by verses, but in the margent: where we [19] shall especially note the speakers, as seemeth more probable, of every parcel, according to the first sense (not having room for more) pertaining to the General spouse, the Catholic Church: which is the great, and everlasting holy City of God the eternal King.

verses.text: LET <na>(a)</na> him kisse me with the kisse of his mouth: because thy brestes are better then wine,

notes.label: a
notes.text: The Church of the old testament desireth Christs coming in flesh: and the Christian Church prayeth for his coming in glorie.

verses.text: smelling fragrantly of the best ointments. Oile powred out is thy name: therfore haue yongmaydes loued thee.

Draw me: we wil runne after thee in the odour of thine ointments. The king hath brought me into his cellars: we wil reioyce & be glad in thee, mindful of thy brests aboue wine: the righteous loue thee.
<na>(b)</na> bI am blacke but beutiful, ô ye daughters of Ierusalem, as the tabernacles of Cedar, as the skinnes of Salomon.

notes.label: b
notes.text: The Church outwardly afflicted, is inwardly fayre.

verses.text: Doe not consider me that I am browne, because the sunne hath altered my colour: the sonnes of my mother haue fought against me, they haue made me a keeper in the vinyards: my vinyard I haue not kept.
Shew me ô thou, whom my soule loueth, where thou feedest, where thou lyest in the midday, lest I beginne to wander after the flockes of thy companyons.
<na>(c)</na> If thou know not thyselfe, ô most fayrest among wemen, goeforth, and folow after the steppes of the flockes, and feede thy kiddes byside the tabernacles of the pastours.

notes.label: c
notes.text: Christ encorageth his spouse the Church.

verses.text: To my companie of horsemen, in the chariotes of Pharao, haue I likened thee, ô my loue.
Thy cheekes are beautiful as the turteldoues, thy necke as iewels.
We wil make thee cheynes of gold, enamoled with siluer.
<na>(d)</na> Whiles the king was at his repose, my spikenard gaue the odour thereof.

notes.label: d
notes.text: She meditateth of his Passion, and Resurrection.

verses.text: A bundle of myrrhe my beloued is to me, he shal abide betwen my brestes.
A clustre of cypre my loue is to me, in the vineyardes of Engaddi.
eBehold thou art fayre, ô my loue, <na>(e)</na> behold thou art fayre, thyne eyes are as of doues.

notes.label: e
notes.text: Christ praiseth his spouse

verses.text: <na>(f)</na> Behold thou art fayre my beloued, & comlie: <na>(g)</na> our litle bed is florishing.

notes.label: f
notes.text: She againe praiseth him;

notes.label: g
notes.text: With thankes for her repose, and present consolation.

verses.text: The beames of our houses are of cedar, our rafters of cypresse trees.
I AM <na>(a)</na> the flower of the filde, and the lilie of the valley.

notes.label: a
notes.text: Christ professeth himself the floure of mankinde: yea Lord of al creatures.

verses.text: <na>(b)</na> As the lilie among the thornes, so is my loue among the daughters.

notes.label: b
notes.text: The Church excelleth al other societies: In the Church the godlie excel sinners, Among the innocent and holie, the virgin Marie surpasseth al.

verses.text: <na>(c)</na> As the apletree among trees of the woddes, so is my beloued among the sonnes. Vnder his shadow, whom I desired, I sate: and his fruite was sweete vnto my throte.

notes.label: c
notes.text: The Church praising Christ resteth secure vnder his protectiõ.

verses.text: He brought me into the winceller, he hath ordered in me charitie.
Stay me vp with flowers, compasse me about with apples: because I languish with loue.
His lefthand vnder my head, and his righthand shal embrace me.
I adiure you ô daughters of Ierusalem, by the roes, and the hartes of the fildes, <na>(d)</na> that you rayse not, nor make the beloued to awake, vntil herselfe wil.

notes.label: d
notes.text: He for the weakes sake permitteth her not to be molested, til she be prepared to suffer with patience.

verses.text: <na>(e)</na> The voice of my beloued, behold he cometh leaping in the mountaines, leaping ouer the little hilles:

notes.label: e
notes.text: She feeling Christs assistance, confesseth, & preacheth boldly his Gospel, & truth against al Paganes, and Heretikes.

verses.text: my beloued is like vnto a roe, and to a fawne of hartes. Behold he standeth behind our walle, <na>(f)</na> looking through the windowes, looking forth by the grates.

notes.label: f
notes.text: Who though he shew not himself visibly:

verses.text: Behold my beloued speaketh to me: <na>(g)</na> Arise, make hast my loue, my doue, beautiful one, and come.

notes.label: g
notes.text: yet encorageth her to approch vnto him:

verses.text: For winter is now past, the rayne is gone, and departed.
The flowers haue appeared in our land, the time of pruning is come: the voice of the turtledoue is heard in our land:
the figgetree hath brought forth her greene figges: the florishing vineyards haue geuen their sauour. Arise my loue, my beautiful one, & come.
My doue in the holes of the rocke, in the holow places of the wal, shew me thy face, let thy voice sound in mine eares: for thy voice is sweete, and thy face comely.
<na>(h)</na> Catch vs the litle foxes, that destroy the vineyards: for our vineyard hath florished.

notes.label: h
notes.text: commandeth his pastors to destroy heresies.

verses.text: <na>(i)</na> My beloued to me, and I to him, who feedeth among the lilies,

notes.label: i
notes.text: And so she reposeth in him.

verses.text: til the day breake, and the shadowes decline. Returne: be like, my beloued, to a roe, and to the fawne of hartes vpon the mountaynes of Bether.
IN <na>(a)</na> my litle bed in the nightes I haue sought him, whom my soule loueth, I haue sought him, and haue not found.

notes.label: a
notes.text: The Church finding Christ not in darke ignorance nor in philosophie but by his reueiling himselfe to her, holdeth him for euer:

verses.text: I wil rise, and wil goe about the citie: by the streates and high waies, I wil seeke him whom my soule loueth: I haue sought him, and haue not found.
The watchmen which kepe the citie found me; Haue you seene him, whom my soule loueth.

When I had a litle passed by them, I found him whom my soule loueth: I held him: neither wil I let him goe, til I bring him into <na>(b)</na> my mothers house, and into the chamber of her that bare me.

notes.label: b
notes.text: euen til the Iewes shal at last also find him.

verses.text: <na>(c)</na> cI adiure you ô daughters of Ierusalem by the roes, and the hartes of the fildes, that you rayse not vp, nor make the beloued to awake, til herselfe wil.

notes.label: c
notes.text: Christ speaketh as before ch. 2. v. 7.

verses.text: <na>(d)</na> What is she, that ascendeth by the desert, as a litle rod of smoke of <na>(e)</na> the aromatical spices of myrtrhe, and frankincense, & of al powder of the apothecharie?

notes.label: d
notes.text: The Church of Christ admireth her owne conuersion from Gentilitie,

notes.label: e
notes.text: now ful of good workes.

verses.text: <na>(f)</na> Behold threescore valiants of the most valiant of Israel, compasse the litle bed of Salomon:

notes.label: f
notes.text: She also professeth that the ascending to eternal rest, is by fighting manfully, in obseruing the ten commandments, in the six dayes of this life:

verses.text: al holding swordes, and most cunning to battels: euerie mans sword vpon his thigh for feares by night.
King Salomon hath made him a portable throne of the wood of Libanus:
the pillers therof he hath made of siluer, the seate of gold, the going vp <na>(g)</na> of purple: the middes he hath paued with <na>(h)</na> charitie for the daughters of Ierusalem.

notes.label: g
notes.text: euen to bloud, if nede be,

notes.label: h
notes.text: which is the highest degree of charitie.

verses.text: <na>(i)</na> Goe forth ye daughters of Sion, and see king Salomon in <na>(k)</na> the diademe, wherewith his mother hath crowned him in the day of his despousing, and in the day of the ioy of his heart.

notes.label: i
notes.text: And inuiteth al others to come vnto Christ,

notes.label: k
notes.text: who in the flesh which he tooke of his mother, was crowned in heauen after his Passion.

verses.text: HOW <na>(a)</na> beautiful art thou my loue, how beautiful art thou! thine <na>(b)</na> eies as it were of doues, besides that, which lyeth hid within. Thy <na>(c)</na> heares as the flockes of goates, which haue come vp from mount Galaad.

notes.label: a
notes.text: Christ againe praieth the beautie of his Church.

notes.label: b
notes.text: Sincere and simple intention.

notes.label: c
notes.text: Al her temporal occupations directed to Gods glorie

verses.text: Thy <na>(d)</na> teeth as flockes of them that are shorne, which haue come vp from the lauatorie, al with <na>(e)</na> twinnes, and there is no barren among them.

notes.label: d
notes.text: Pastors who like nurces geue bread of good doctrine to litle ones.

notes.label: e
notes.text: Faith and good workes.

verses.text: Thy <na>(f)</na> lippes as a scarlet lace: and thy speach sweete. As à peece of a pomegranate, so are also thy <na>(g)</na> cheekes, besides that which lyeth hid within.

notes.label: f
notes.text: Preaching Christs passion.

notes.label: g
notes.text: And not ashamed to professe Christ Crucified.

verses.text: Thy <na>(h)</na> necke is as the <na>(i)</na> towre of Dauid, which is built with bulworkes: a thousand targattes hang on it, al the armour of the valiants.

notes.label: h
notes.text: Administration of Sacraments wherby the Church, Christs mystical bodie, is ioyned to him her head,

notes.label: i
notes.text: which is an inexpugnable fortresse.

verses.text: Thy <na>(k)</na> two breastes as two fawnes the twinnes of a roe, which feede among the lilies,

notes.label: k
notes.text: Both Iewes and Gentiles are fed with the principles of Christian doctrin.

verses.text: til the day aspire, and the shadowes decline. <na>(l)</na> lI wil goe to the mount of myrrhe, and to the little hil of frankencense.

notes.label: l
notes.text: Christ dwelleth in mortified, and deuout mindes.

verses.text: Thou art al fayre ô my loue, and there is <na>(m)</na> not a spotte in thee.

notes.label: m
notes.text: The Church triumphant is without spotte, and euerie particular soule entring into heauen; the B. virgin mother was also in this life alwayes immaculate.

verses.text: Come from Libanus my spouse, come from Libanus, come: thou shalt be crowned from the head of Amena, from the toppe of Sanir & Hermon, from the dennes of lions, from the mountaynes of leopardes.
Thou hast wounded my heart, my sister spouse, thou hast wounded my heart in one of thine eies, and in one heare of thy necke.
How beautiful are thy breastes my sister spouse! thy breastes are more beautiful then wine, and the odour of thine ointmentes aboue al aromatical spices.
Thy lippes my spouse are as an honie combe distilling, honie and milke are vnder thy tongue: and the odour of thy garments as the odour of frankincense.
My sister spouse is a garden inclosed, a garden inclosed, a fountaine sealed vp.
Thy offsprings a paradise of pomegranats with orchard fruites. Cypres with spiknard,
spiknard, and safren, sweete cane and cinnamon, with al the trees of Libanus, myrrhe and aloes with al the chiefe ointmentes.
The fountaine of gardens: the wel of liuing waters, which runne with violence from Libanus.
<na>(n)</na> Arise Northwinde, & come Southwinde, blow through my garden, and let the aromatical spices therof flowe.

notes.label: n
notes.text: Al tentations, whether they be in manifest crueltie, or in flatering suteltie, make constant soules more gratful to God.

verses.text: LET <na>(a)</na> my beloued come into his garden, and eate the fruite of his appletrees. <na>(b)</na> bI am come into my garden ô my sister spouse, I haue reaped my myrrhe, with myne aromatical spices: I haue eaten the honiecombe with mine honie, I haue drunke my wine with my milke: <na>(c)</na> eate ô frendes, and drinke, and be inebriated my dearest.

notes.label: a
notes.text: The spouse condescending to Gods wil, is wel content to suffer persecution.

notes.label: b
notes.text: Christ againe sheweth his good liking in his spouses patience:

notes.label: c
notes.text: and willeth the glorious Sainctes to congratulate with the patient.

verses.text: <na>(d)</na> dI sleepe, and my hart watcheth: <na>(e)</na> the voice of my beloued knocking: Open to me my sister, my loue, my doue, mine immaculate: <na>(f)</na> because my head is ful of dew, and my lockes of the droppes of the nightes.

notes.label: d
notes.text: The spouse desireth to rest in meditation.

notes.label: e
notes.text: but is called vpon to helpe others:

notes.label: f
notes.text: and vrged by Christs owne example working for al mankind.

verses.text: I haue spoyled myselfe of my robe, how shal I be clothed with it? I haue washed my feete, how shal I defile them?
My beloued put his hand through the hôle, and my bellie trembled at his touch.
<na>(g)</na> gI arose, that I might open to my beloued: my handes haue distilled myrrhe, and my fingers are ful of most approued myrrhe.

notes.label: g
notes.text: And so she imployeth herself also in actiue life.

verses.text: I opened the bolt of my dore to my beloued: but he had turned aside, and was passed. My soule melted, as he spake: I sought, and found him not: I called, and he did not answer me.
The keepers that goe about the citie found me: they stroke me, and wounded me: the keepers of the walles tooke away my cloke.
<na>(h)</na> hI adiure you ô daughters of Hierusalem, if you shal finde my beloued, that you tel him, that I languishe with loue.

notes.label: h
notes.text: Stil conseruing a desire to returne vnto contemplation.

verses.text: <na>(i)</na> What maner of one is thy beloued of the beloued, ô most beautiful of wemen? What maner of one is thy beloued of the beloued, that thou hast so adiured vs?

notes.label: i
notes.text: The deuout confer together describing the excellencies of Christ.

verses.text: My beloued is white and ruddie, chosen of thousands.
His head is as the best gold: his heares as the branches of palmetrees, blacke as à rauen.
His eies as doues vpon the litle riuers of waters, which are washed with milke, and sitte beside the most ful streames.
His cheekes are as litle beddes of aromatical spices set of the pigmentaries. His lippes are as lilies distilling principal myrrhe.
His handes wrought round of gold, ful of hyacinthes. His bellie of iuorie, distinguished with sapphires.
His thighes as pillers of marble, that are vpon feete of gold. His forme as of Libanus, elect as the cedars.
His throte most sweete, and he whole to be desired: such an one is my beloued, and he is my frend, ô daughters of Hierusalem.
<na>(k)</na> Whither is thy beloued gone ô most beautiful of wemen? whither is thy beloued turned aside, and we wil seeke him with thee?

notes.label: k
notes.text: And resolue to seke him, wheresoeuer he be.

verses.text: MY <na>(a)</na> beloued is gone downe into his garden, to the bed of aromatical spices, to feede in the gardens, and to gather lilies.

notes.label: a
notes.text: The Church teacheth her children that Christ is delighted with the godlie desires, and fructful workes of the faithful.

verses.text: I to my beloued, and my beloued to me, who feedeth among the lilies.
<na>(b)</na> Thou art fayre ô my loue, sweete, and comelie as Hierusalem: terrible as the armie of a campe set in aray.

notes.label: b
notes.text: Christ againe commendeth his Church, wel composed of distinct orders (some gouerning, some retired in cloisters from this world, the rest also exercising workes of mercie, in the trubles of this life) al together making a complete armie, terrible to al enimies.

verses.text: <na>(c)</na> Turne away thine eies from me, because they haue made me flee away. Thy heares as a flocke of goates, which haue appeared from Galaad.

notes.label: c
notes.text: The more anie contemplate Gods Maiestie, the better they perceiue that he is incomprehensible.

verses.text: Thy teeth as à flocke of sheepe, which haue come vp from the lauatorie, al with twinnes, and there is no barren among them.
As the barke of a pomegranate, so are thy cheekes beside thy hidden.
There are <na>(d)</na> threescore queenes, & <na>(e)</na> fourescore concubines, and of <na>(f)</na> fyongmaydes there is no number.

notes.label: d
notes.text: Manie true pastores,

notes.label: e
notes.text: more hyrelinges, that also preach truth, but for temporal commoditie.

notes.label: f
notes.text: And innumerable faithful soules in the Church.

verses.text: My doue is <na>(g)</na> one, my perfect one, she is the only to her mother, elect to her that bare her. The daughters haue seene her, and declared her to be most blessed: the queenes and concubines, and haue praysed her.

notes.label: g
notes.text: Al which are but one bodie in vnitie of faith.

verses.text: <na>(h)</na> What is she, that cometh forth as the morning rysing, fayre as the moone, elect as the sunne, terrible as the armie of a campe set in aray?

notes.label: h
notes.text: The voice of the old synagogue, admiring the beautie of Christs Church.

verses.text: I came downe into the garden of nuttes, to see the fruites of the valles, and to looke if the vineyarde had florished, and the pomegranats budded.
I knew not: my soule trubled me for the chariotes of Aminadab.
<na>(i)</na> Returne, returne ô Sulamitesse: returne, returne that we may behold thee.

notes.label: i
notes.text: The Church of Christ exhorteth the Synagogue of the Iewes to returne to Christ.

verses.text: WHAT <na>(a)</na> shalt thou see in the Sulamitesse but the companies of campes? How beautiful are thy pases in shoes, ô princes daughter! <na>(b)</na> the ioyntes of thy thighes are as iewels, that are made by the hand of the artificer.

notes.label: a
notes.text: Christ interposeth his commendation of the Iewes, who at last shal returne to him with great feruoure of faith and deuotion.

notes.label: b
notes.text: And so iointly praiseth his Church consisting of both peoples.

verses.text: Thy nauel as à round bowle, neuer wanting cuppes. Thy bellie as an heape of wheate, compassed about with lilies.
Thy two brests, as two fawnes the twinnes of a roe.
Thy necke as a towre of yuorie. Thine eies as the fishpooles in Hesebon, which are in the gate of the daughter of the multitude. Thy nose as the towre of Libanus; that looketh against Damascus.
Thy head as Carmelus: and the heares of thy head as a kings purple tyed to cundite pipes.
How beautiful art thou, and how comely my dearest, in delightes!
Thy stature is like to a palmetree, & thy breastes to clusters of grapes.
I sayd: I wil goe vp into the palmetree, and wil take hold of the fruites therof: and thy breasts shal be as the clusters of a vineyard: and the odour of thy mouth as it were of apples.
Thy throate as the best wine, <na>(c)</na> worthie for my beloued to drinke, & for his lippes and his teeth to ruminate.

notes.label: c
notes.text: The Church, as it were taking the word out of Christs mouth whiles he praised her, she returneth al the praise to him.

verses.text: I to my beloued, and his turning is toward me.
<na>(d)</na> Come my beloued, let vs goe forth in to the filde, let vs abide in the villages.

notes.label: d
notes.text: Praying him to come and stil remaine with her.

verses.text: Let vs rise early to the vineyards, let vs see if the vineyard florishe, if the flowers be readie to bring forth fruites, if the pomegranates florish: there wil I giue thee my breasts.
The Mandragoraes haue geuen a smel. In our gates al fruites: <na>(e)</na> the new and the old, my beloued, I haue kept for thee.

notes.label: e
notes.text: Acknowleging him to be the only Sauiour of both old and new testament.

verses.text: WHO <na>(a)</na> shal giue to me thee my brother, sucking the breasts of my mother, that I may finde thee without, and kisse thee, and now no man despise me?

notes.label: a
notes.text: The Synagogue prosecuteth her prayer, desiring Christs Incarnation.

verses.text: I wil take hold of thee, and wil bring thee into my mothers house: there thou shalt teach me, and I wil giue thee a cuppe of spiced wine, and new wine of my pomegranats.
His left hand vnder my head, and his right hand shal embrace me.
<na>(b)</na> bI adiure you ô daughters of Ierusalem, that you rayse not vp, nor make the beloued to awake til herselfe wil.

notes.label: b
notes.text: Christ admonisheth wordlie men not to molest those that serue him in contemplation, & other spiritual vertues.

verses.text: <na>(c)</na> Who is this, that cometh vp from the desert, flowing with delightes, leaning vpon her beloued? Vnder the appletree I raysed thee vp: <na>(d)</na> there thy mother was corrupted, there she was defloured that bare thee.

notes.label: c
notes.text: Angels and other Sainctes of the triumphant Church admire the beautie of the Gentiles conuerted; which is also vnderstood of euerie holie soule ascending from this world into heauen, And more singularly of the most glorious virgin mother of God.

notes.label: d
notes.text: The Synagogue of the Iewes was corrupt vnder the tree of Christs Crosse, when they cried: Crucifie him, Crucifie him. And againe: His bloud be vpon vs, and vpon our children. Againe: We haue no King but Cæsar. &c.

verses.text: Put me as a seale vpon thy hart, as a seale vpon thyne arme: because loue is strong as death: ielousie is hard as hel, the lampes therof lampes of fyre and flames.
Manie waters can not quench charitie, neither shal floudes ouerwhelme it: if a man shal giue al the substance of his house for loue, as nothing he shal despise it.
<na>(e)</na> Our sister is litle, and hath no breasts. What shal we doe to our sister in the day when she is to be spoken vnto?

notes.label: e
notes.text: Christ againe sheweth his affection towards his Church of the Gentiles: calling her his owne sister, and the Synagogs sister, promising and bestowing on her manie excellent benefites.

verses.text: If she be a wal, let vs build vpon it bulwarkes of siluer: if she be a doore, let vs ioyne it together with bordes of ceder.
<na>(f)</na> fI am a wal: and my breasts are as a towre, since I was made before him as one finding peace.

notes.label: f
notes.text: The Church of Gentiles reioyceth in the strong defence, wherwith her Sauiour hath established her.

verses.text: The peacemaker had a vinyard, in that which hath peoples: he deliuered the same <na>(g)</na> to keepers, a man bringeth for the fruite thereof a thousand peeces of siluer.

notes.label: g
notes.text: Keepers of this vinyard, were the Prophetes and Apostles, and their Successors are stil the kepers therof.

verses.text: <na>(h)</na> My vineyard is before me. A thousand are thy peacemakers, and two hundreth for them, that keepe the fruites thereof.

notes.label: h
notes.text: Christ sheweth that together with the pastors, himself especially hath care of his Church, alwayes assisting the visible gouerners therof with his inuisible grace.

verses.text: Thou that dwellest in the gardens, the frends doe harken: make me heare thy voice.
<na>(i)</na> Flee, ô my beloued, and be like to the roe, and to the fawne of harts vpon the mountaines of aromatical spices.

notes.label: i
notes.text: The whole Church militant wel contented, yea desiring Christs Ascension into heauen, for the good of al that here serue him, prayeth him from thence to send abundance of his grace, that we may ascend the high mountaines of perfect charitie, and zele of Gods honour, that he wil make our soules such hilles, the garden of al vertues, & so voutsafe to dwel therin. Amen.
